spec.title: Lens execution architecture: native subagents and managed terminals

status.comment: Owner clarification of 2026-09-15: Codex is the initial test host; native children remain the baseline, while externally orchestrated interactive managed agents are the intended extensible mode. Architecture update only; managed terminals, RLM orchestration and remote hosts are not implemented by this document.

p.terminology: Native subagents are children created and controlled through the coordinator's own agent harness. Managed agents are independent agent processes launched and supervised by Lens execution infrastructure, with real interactive virtual terminals that an authorized human can inspect and control. Role (coordinator or worker), launch origin (Lens or user), subagent ownership mode (native or managed), agent product/model, interaction transport and execution host are separately recorded dimensions whose valid combinations are capability-constrained. The initial managed mode requires a Lens-owned launch; merely joining a user-started session does not transfer process or terminal ownership. Starting a coordinator through Codex app-server does not turn its native children into managed agents. Earlier references to managed coordinators in PROP-005 research mean Lens-supervised coordinator sessions, not the managed-terminal mode defined here.

p.native-baseline: Project coordination, ordinary agent chat, ZapAskUserQuestion, history, plan control and the shared Lens clients must remain usable with native subagents and with managed execution disabled or absent. Native lifecycle and child controls reflect the actual harness capabilities; Lens does not invent a terminal or independently controllable process for a native child. Codex is the first implementation and test product. Other products remain registered adapter capabilities rather than assumptions embedded in the common model. Native-only deployment is a supported configuration, not a temporary stub dependent on managed-terminal code.

p.availability-policy: Enabled execution modes are the intersection of configured deployment policy, supported adapter capabilities, project scope and granted authority. A native-only profile does not advertise or dispatch managed launches. Unavailable modes or orchestration features return explicit unsupported or policy-denied results; no silent cross-mode or cross-provider fallback spends resources or circumvents the selected policy. This configuration supports changing product or licensing constraints without asserting that a particular provider currently permits or forbids a mode. Existing session continuity and a new run's mode selection are separate; changing a selector never converts an in-flight native child into a managed terminal.

p.authority-boundaries: The shared Lens server owns execution control: project/context registries, logical actors, tasks, run attempts, coordinator sessions, dispatch/admission queues, leases, budgets and durable execution history. An agent-host supervisor owns local processes and terminal handles and reports observed facts. A strategy proposes how to decompose, route and join work. ZAP remains the authority for the semantic plan, economics, holds and admitted plan changes. Execution scheduling does not become a second planning engine, and a process exit or strategy self-report does not establish task acceptance.

p.execution-identities: A logical task is distinct from a run attempt, agent actor, conversation/session and host process. Stable records bind project/context, task and parent task, run/attempt, actor, coordinator, product profile, execution mode, host, workspace binding and source/plan basis. Native thread/session IDs, process identifiers and terminal IDs remain adapter-owned correlation with explicit incarnation epochs. Multiple attempts may serve one task without overwriting earlier results. Parentage and project authority are validated independently of display names or process trees.

p.work-packets: Delegated work uses a host-neutral packet containing the goal, selected context and artifact references, expected result contract, source/plan basis, available capabilities, resource limits, parent/depth and routing preferences. The coordinator follows the full applicable project boot and retains its long-lived session. Workers receive the context required for their packet rather than an automatic copy of the entire coordinator boot or every sibling transcript. Result artifacts, public summaries and acceptance evidence are distinct from console output. Concrete operating-system paths and protected environment construction are resolved by the selected host, not hardcoded in portable work packets.

p.execution-backends: A NativeSubagentBackend requests or observes coordinator-driven native delegation and maps supported harness lifecycle, messages and results into the common run model. A ManagedAgentBackend admits a registered launch profile through an AgentHost and creates an owned interactive terminal session for the worker. Both share actor addressing, questions, history, cancellation intent, result references and plan basis. Supported controls are capability-described rather than forced into an identical native API. The agent-product adapter, subagent mode and execution-host placement remain independently selectable.

p.managed-terminal: Managed-terminal execution runs the actual interactive agent CLI/TUI in a real virtual terminal using the platform's supported pseudoterminal facility. It retains duplex input, terminal output, dimensions and lifecycle; an ordinary pipe containing headless JSON output is not represented as a live terminal. Structured agent events or APIs may supplement interaction where supported, while the terminal remains the actual session visible to the user. Terminal capabilities include inspect, subscribe, request input control, write, resize, interrupt and release control. The supervisor owns the registered agent process/tree; ending that agent does not leave an unrestricted shell as the next input target.

p.input-control: Many Lens clients may observe a managed terminal, but exactly one authorized controller owns its input lease at a time: the automation dispatcher or one human client. Acquiring human control fences previous automation input by epoch before accepting human bytes. Already running work continues unless an explicit interrupt is requested; input ownership is not the same as stopping execution. Human and automated input are attributed and ordered. Returning control is explicit, with the new context or intervention made available to the coordinator. Disconnect or uncertain partial delivery does not silently replay terminal bytes or resume competing automation. Terminal resize also has an authoritative owner so observers cannot fight over session dimensions.

p.terminal-evidence: The terminal view shows real observed output rather than reconstructed assistant messages. Terminal bytes, screen checkpoints, input attribution, dimensions and process/session epochs are distinct artifact streams with cursor and coverage information. Reconnecting a viewer resumes this stream where retained; it does not prove that a dead process or lost PTY can be revived. Structured chat, question, plan and execution events retain their own provenance. A terminal string that looks like a completion or approval is not by itself an authoritative ZAP event. Protected/raw capture and any redacted display are identified honestly; credential values are not ordinary public history payloads.

p.supervision: Execution control records a stable launch claim before provisioning or starting a process. The host registers run/session identity, owns the process tree, reports lifecycle and available usage, and accepts scoped interruption or cancellation requests. Requested, accepted, observed exit and judged completion remain separate states. Host/control-plane reconnect reconciles the existing run before another launch; missing contact means unknown status until resolved, not immediate success or safe duplication. Viewer lifetime is independent of process lifetime. Durable state and supervisor policy specify what survives server, supervisor or worker failure; Fractality's kill-on-supervisor-close behavior is evidence for one policy, not a universal reconnect guarantee.

p.strategy-extension: Orchestration strategies consume scoped goals, context/result references, run state and budgets and propose work packets, dependency edges, routing, joins, local context processing or escalation. They cannot directly spawn processes, write terminal bytes, obtain credentials or bypass execution/ZAP admission. RLM-style recursive context decomposition and result aggregation is a future strategy above this seam; native delegation and ordinary managed fan-out can use simpler strategies. Context-by-reference, explicit sibling-result access, recursion budgets and aggregation contracts are architectural requirements; a learned router or full RLM implementation is not part of the initial MVP.

p.execution-hosts: An AgentHost identifies the environment that executes a registered profile and resolves its workspace and artifacts. The MVP uses one local host. Future remote hosts implement the same scoped launch, observation, control and artifact contracts with independent host/session epochs; native local absolute paths or PIDs are not portable identifiers. Remote authentication, workspace provisioning, artifact transfer and scheduling are deferred implementations, not capabilities inferred from the presence of a hostId field. Product mixing and placement decisions belong to strategy/policy rather than Lens presentation code.

p.shared-clients: Quicklens, Gamelens and Codlens VS Code/IDEA integrations use the same execution services and actor/run graph. They may expose chat, inbox, history, agent tree and managed terminal in different layouts. Native children show their real available status, messages and results; managed workers additionally expose their terminal capability. Opening another client or board does not launch another actor, transfer input ownership or alter another window's project focus. Terminal rendering and native IDE integration are presentation/host bridges; execution authority remains on the shared server and AgentHost.

p.network-and-control: The localhost agent channel and authenticated HTTPS UI gateway remain separate. Managed-terminal observation and input are named, separately authorized capabilities scoped to an existing project, session, host and control epoch. Enabling chat or logging into Quicklens alone does not grant terminal input. The managed module may expose authorized terminal control through the UI gateway when configured; it never exposes an arbitrary shell/process/proxy endpoint or a raw host-agent listener. The rule against injecting input into unrelated user terminals remains. Sending bytes through an explicitly owned managed PTY is an intended, visible control operation.

p.fractality-transfer: Fractality is an architectural reference for mission control, per-run supervisors, work packets, journaled launch claims, resource limits, claim-check results and recovery. Its inspected prototype launches headless Claude Code with piped streams and one-shot stdin; it does not implement the managed interactive terminal required here. Study findings are recorded in LENS-EXECUTION-ARCHITECTURE-2026-09-15.md. Lens takes these boundaries as design input; it does not import the old Claude-specific launcher, retired provider subscription, historical research harness or entire Fractality product as a runtime dependency.

p.delivery-order: First revise common Lens contracts and shared-server ownership, then complete the Codex coordinator/native-child prototype with chat, rich questions, history and multiple project views. Next add an explicitly enabled local managed-terminal prototype demonstrating a real agent console, human observation, input-control transfer and ordinary completion reporting. Both modes must remain available according to configuration. Only later add mixed agent products, remote hosts and RLM strategy implementation. Verification is bounded to the demonstrated path and required project checks; no exhaustive host matrix, comparative pilot or unrelated edge-case refinement is authorized by this architecture update.
